etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English tellen (“to count, tell”), from Old English tellan (“to count, tell”), from Proto-West Germanic *talljan, from Proto-Germanic *taljaną, *talzijaną (“to count, enumerate”), from Proto-Germanic *talą, *talǭ (“number, counting”), from Proto-Indo-European *dol- (“calculation, fraud”).

Cognate with Saterland Frisian tälle (“to say; tell”), West Frisian telle (“to count”), West Frisian fertelle (“to tell, narrate”), Dutch tellen (“to count”) and Dutch vertellen (“to tell”), Low German tellen (“to count”), German zählen, Faroese telja. More at tale.

definitions.definition: (transitive, archaic outside of idioms) To count, reckon, or enumerate.

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book II, Canto VII”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
quote.text: And in his lap a masse of coyne he told,  And turned vpsidowne, to feede his eye  A couetous desire with his huge threasury.

quote.citation: c. 1589–1590 (date written), Christopher Marlo[we], edited by Tho[mas] Heywood, The Famous Tragedy of the Rich Iew of Malta. […], London:  […]  I[ohn] B[eale] for Nicholas Vavasour, […], published 1633, →OCLC, Act I:
quote.text: Well fare the Arabians, who so richly payThe things they traffic for with wedge of gold,Whereof a man may easily in a dayTell that which may maintain him all his life.

quote.citation: 1875, Hugh MacMillan, The Sunday Magazine:
quote.text: Only He who made them can tell the number of the stars, and mark the place of each in the order of the one great dominant spiral.

quote.citation: 1918, W[illiam] B[abington] Maxwell, chapter VII, in The Mirror and the Lamp, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: “ […] Churchill, my dear fellow, we have such greedy sharks, and wolves in lamb's clothing. Oh, dear, there's so much to tell you, so many warnings to give you, but all that must be postponed for the moment.”

definitions.definition: (transitive, ditransitive) To convey by speech; to say.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter IV, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: I told him about everything I could think of; and what I couldn't think of he did. He asked about six questions during my yarn, but every question had a point to it. At the end he bowed and thanked me once more. As a thanker he was main-truck high; I never see anybody so polite.

quote.citation: 2016, VOA Learning English (public domain)
quote.text:
Tell her you’re here.
Audio (US):(file)

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Genesis xii:18:
quote.text: Why didst thou not tell me that she was thy wife?

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter V, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC:
quote.text: But Miss Thorn relieved the situation by laughing aloud, […] . We began to tell her about Mohair and the cotillon, and of our point of observation from the Florentine galleried porch, and she insisted she would join us there.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To order; to direct, to say to someone.

quote.citation: 1909, H. G. Wells, Ann Veronica:
quote.text: She said she hoped she had not distressed him by the course she had felt obliged to take, and he told her not to be a fool.

quote.citation: 2012 October 25, John Noble Wilford, “Neil Armstrong, First Man on the Moon, Dies at 82”, in New York Times‎[1]:
quote.text: Stability was restored, but once the re-entry propulsion was activated, the crew was told to prepare to come home before the end of their only day in orbit.

quote.citation: 2022 January 12, Benedict le Vay, “The heroes of Soham...”, in RAIL, number 948:
quote.text: The driver remained at his post, while telling fireman Jim Nightall to get down on the track and run back to uncouple the burning wagon from the rest.

definitions.definition: (transitive or intransitive) To discern, notice, identify or distinguish.

quote.citation: 1910, Emerson Hough, chapter I, in The Purchase Price: Or The Cause of Compromise, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: Captain Edward Carlisle, soldier as he was, martinet as he was, felt a curious sensation of helplessness seize upon him as he met her steady gaze, her alluring smile; he could not tell what this prisoner might do.

quote.citation: 1990, Stephen Coonts, Under Siege, 1991 Pocket Books edition, →ISBN, p.409:
quote.text: Cherry looks old, Mergenthaler told himself. His age is telling. Querulous — that's the word. He's become a whining, querulous old man absorbed with trivialities.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To have an effect, especially a noticeable one; to be apparent, to be demonstrated.

quote.citation: 1859, John Stuart Mill, On Liberty:
quote.text: Opinion ought [… to give] merited honour to every one, whatever opinion he may hold […] keeping nothing back which tells, or can be supposed to tell, in their favour.

quote.citation: 1960 April, Cecil J. Allen, “Locomotive Running Past and Present”, in Trains Illustrated, page 212:
quote.text: [...] the 4 miles at 1 in 180 up to Sanquhar were mounted with no greater fall in speed than from 65 to 59 m.p.h., after which, possibly as a result of easing the engine or because the strain on steam supply was beginning to tell, the final 3½ miles up at 1 in 200 up to milepost 59½ were surmounted at a minimum of 49½ m.p.h.

quote.citation: 2011 September 18, Ben Dirs, “Rugby World Cup 2011: England 41-10 Georgia”, in BBC Sport:
quote.text: But England's superior fitness told in the second half, with Delon Armitage, Manu Tuilagi and Chris Ashton (two) going over for tries to secure a bonus-point win.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To use (beads or similar objects) as an aid to prayer.
(intransitive, childish) To inform someone in authority about a wrongdoing.
(authorship, intransitive) To reveal information in prose through outright expository statement — contrasted with show.

A reflexive, often habitual behavior, especially one occurring in a context that often features attempts at deception by persons under psychological stress (such as a poker game or police interrogation), that reveals information that the person exhibiting the behavior is attempting to withhold.
(informal) A giveaway; something that unintentionally reveals or hints at a secret.

quote.citation: 2023 May 4, Amy X. Wang, Grant Cornett, “Inside the Delirious Rise of ‘Superfake’ Handbags”, in The New York Times‎[2], →ISSN:
quote.text: Those whose business it is to verify luxury bags insist, at least publicly, that there’s always a “tell” to a superfake.

quote.citation: 2024 January 3, John Patrick Leary, “Israel's "Right to Exist" Is a Rhetorical Trap”, in The New Republic‎[3]:
quote.text: Republican Congressman Chris Smith of New Jersey said recently that “Israel is the only state in the world whose fundamental right to exist, within any borders at all, is openly denied by other states.” But Israel is the only nation with a “right to exist,” as the phrase is not commonly attached to any other country. And that’s the tell: This is not a legal concept, but a political one, available for broad interpretation and rhetorical weaponization.

definitions.definition: (archaic) That which is told; a tale or account.

quote.citation: April 4, 1743, Horace Walpole, letter to Sir Horace Mann
quote.text: I am at the end of my tell.

definitions.definition: (Internet) A private message to an individual in a chat room; a whisper.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Arabic تَلّ (tall, “hill, elevation”) or Hebrew תֵּל (tél, “hill”), from Proto-Semitic *tall- (“hill”).

definitions.definition: (archaeology) A hill or mound, originally and especially in the Middle East, over or consisting of the ruins of ancient settlements.

quote.citation: 2001, David L. Lieber, Jules Harlow, Etz Hayim: Torah and Commentary, page 205:
quote.text: Succoth is now associated with a large tell situated in the Jordan Valley, Deir Allah.
